prize_parts.citation: For their theory of strategic bargaining, including the alternating-offers model and its extension to bargaining in decentralised markets.

statement.case_for: Rubinstein's 1982 alternating-offers model gave bargaining a tractable non-cooperative foundation with a unique subgame-perfect outcome. The Rubinstein-Wolinsky market-bargaining work carried that logic into decentralised trade, which links it to search, matching and price formation. The contribution is conceptual and portable. It is used in labour, trade, industrial organisation, macro search models and political economy, and its influence has been confirmed over more than forty years. Attribution is also comparatively clean: Rubinstein for the core model, Wolinsky for the market extension. On maturity, the main risk is that recognition is overdue, not that it is premature. After the round of openings I keep B001 first. I do not rest this on its support count, which is moderate. It rests on the depth and durability of the result and the clarity of its credit, which compare well with the younger or more diffusely credited candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that bargaining theory sits in a field already honoured many times (Nash, Harsanyi and Selten, Aumann, Schelling, Myerson, Maskin and Hurwicz, Milgrom and Wilson), and several colleagues think this crowds the case. The model's direct empirical bite is also limited, and a committee that weights demonstrated policy or empirical impact could fairly rank the labour and public-economics candidates higher. The credit structure is not fully settled. Rubinstein's central result is essentially single-authored, Wolinsky's share rests on the market-bargaining extension, and Binmore's Nash-programme work and Ståhl's earlier finite-horizon results complicate the lineage. My own training is in market design, so I may overrate theory that sits next to it.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B030 (BLP and dynamic industry models) first. He argues the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core is cleanly attributable, standard in antitrust and empirical IO, and mature, and that Bresnahan would dilute a clear core. He also asks whether bargaining is distinct enough from earlier game-theory prizes.
responses.response: I agree that the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes attribution is clean and that the tools are heavily used in practice, which is why I ranked B030 sixth and not lower. I still see the contribution as an estimation methodology that makes market power measurable, and its dynamic-model branch has seen mixed practical adoption. Bargaining theory is a conceptual foundation that other fields build on. On his prior-prize concern, I accept the point but think it is weaker than it looks. The earlier game-theory awards were for equilibrium and refinement theory, incomplete information, and mechanism design. Rubinstein's work is a positive model of how negotiation itself unfolds, which none of them covers. I agree with him that Binmore is the weaker claim, so I would keep him out.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B041 (firm heterogeneity and trade) first with a Melitz-Helpman core. He notes that recent prizes have favoured mechanism design and auctions, that Rubinstein is the clear originator, and that Binmore's role is secondary.
responses.response: We agree on Rubinstein and on Binmore's secondary role. I disagree that the auction and mechanism-design prizes absorb bargaining. I gave the 2020 presentation speech on auctions, so I know how far that prize was about designing allocation rules. The alternating-offers result belongs to a different branch, the strategic microfoundations of price formation. On B041, I proposed Melitz alone in my opening because Melitz is the clear originator. I accept that adding Helpman through the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension is a fair reading of the ballot. I still find the trade candidates harder to settle. Helpman also appears in B013, and Krugman's 2008 prize already covered the monopolistic-competition foundation. The trade-theory space is therefore less clear than the bargaining case.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B002 first with Chetty and Hendren only. She stresses large-sample administrative data, credible quasi-experimental design, and the lack of room for Friedman and Katz under a cap.
responses.response: Her two-person version moves me. My opening named Friedman as the third laureate, but the case for him rests on data infrastructure and team contributions, which is the weakest part of the attribution. The Chetty-Hendren pair has the clearest claim on the causal place-effects work. If B002 is taken up, I would back Chetty and Hendren over a three-name list. I still hold it below B001 because of maturity. Most of the evidence comes from after 2014. The long-run causal reading of neighbourhood effects is still debated, and replication depends on restricted data. Enflo, Friberg and Hassler raise similar timing concerns.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 first. She credits it with new data plus an explanatory framework, large societal impact, and a core finding that has become standard despite debate over magnitudes. She notes the choice of three names is difficult, particularly Katz.
responses.response: I rank B038 third and agree it is a strong, mature candidate. On attribution, I keep Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the coherent trio, because the China-shock programme is theirs. Adding Katz, as Fredriksson and Krusell do, would anchor the prize in the earlier skill-demand literature, and it would reopen the task-framework lineage (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu) that Boppart and Friberg also flag. I would define the prize by the China-shock programme and not by a combined tasks-and-trade rationale, because the combination makes the citation less coherent. Disputes over the size and persistence of the shock, together with the 2023 and 2024 prizes on adjacent labour and technology topics, keep me from ranking it above the bargaining result.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues will treat prior game-theory recognition as grounds against a bargaining prize, or as irrelevant to a distinct branch.
Whether the right set of laureates is Rubinstein with Wolinsky, Rubinstein alone, or a set that includes Binmore. Ståhl's earlier finite-horizon work is a further priority complication.
Whether B002 is mature enough, and whether Friedman or Katz has a stronger claim than a Chetty-Hendren pair.
How to weigh a conceptual theory prize against empirical candidates with documented policy influence, without letting my own field proximity decide it.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. None of my listed co-authors or networks (Svensson, Ehlers, Erlanson, Martinello, Teytelboym, Trapp, Biró) appears among the credited names on the shortlist. I disclose that my field, market and mechanism design, is adjacent to bargaining and matching theory, and that I gave the 2020 presentation speech on auction theory. That speech reflects Academy drafting and does not show a preference for any 2026 candidate. My SSE affiliation with Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg is a colleague connection, not a candidate connection.
